data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"Single-evaluation evidence that the panel's confidence tracks correctness more tightly than the expert's\u2014specifically, that the panel is well-calibrated *on the divergence stratum*\u2014would indicate a genuine reliability gain, because mere checklist compliance does not produce calibrated confidence on cases where intuition and rule conflict.","counterconditions":[{"case":"The panel is well-calibrated on the agreement stratum but miscalibrated on the divergence stratum (calibration does not transfer to the critical cases).","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"The panel's confidence is an artifact of checklist-completion rate (high confidence = all boxes ticked) rather than genuine meta-monitoring.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"The expert is also well-calibrated on the divergence stratum (the panel's calibration advantage disappears where it matters).","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Mere checklist compliance can produce correct answers without calibrated confidence: the panel ticks boxes and outputs the indicated answer, but its confidence does not track the probability of correctness. Genuine reliability requires the panel to *know when the checklist's rule is reliable and when it is not*. This is revealed by calibration analysis on the divergence stratum: if the panel's confidence predicts its accuracy (good calibration) specifically on cases where the checklist and the expert disagree, the panel is not merely complying but is meta-monitoring the checklist's applicability. If the panel is overconfident on divergence cases it gets right (lucky compliance) and underconfident on those it gets wrong, it lacks genuine calibration.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
